summary: As the women run from the empty tomb, the risen Jesus meets them, receives their worship, and sends word to His brethren to meet Him in Galilee.
key_insight: The disciples had all forsaken Jesus and fled (Matthew 26:56). Yet when the risen Jesus first speaks of them in Matthew, He calls them “My brethren.”
story: At dawn on the first day of the week, the women had found the stone rolled away and heard the angel say that Jesus was risen. They went out quickly from the tomb “with fear and great joy,” and ran to bring His disciples word.
As they went, Jesus Himself met them. He greeted them with a single word: “Rejoice!” They came to Him, took hold of His feet and worshiped Him.
Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid. Go and tell My brethren to go to Galilee, and there they will see Me.”

fit.question: Matthew names Mary Magdalene among the women who came to the tomb, then says Jesus met “them” on the way. But John tells of Mary meeting Jesus alone in the garden, and Mark says He appeared “first to Mary Magdalene” (Mark 16:9). Was she with the women on the road?

points.label: Mary ran ahead
points.text: John says that as soon as Mary Magdalene saw the stone taken away, she ran to tell Peter and John (John 20:1–2). She probably left before the other women heard the angel. She then came back to the tomb behind Peter and John, and there Jesus met her alone (John 20:11–18).

points.label: Matthew tells it briefly
points.text: Matthew names only two women and tells the whole morning in a few lines. He speaks of the women as one group and does not track who left when. His “them” means the women who carried the angel’s message, without claiming that every woman who set out at dawn was there.

points.label: Who saw Him first
points.text: Mark says the women who fled the tomb were afraid and at first “said nothing to anyone” (Mark 16:8). Some harmonies suggest this delay left room for Jesus to meet Mary first and the other women soon after.

fit.note: The Gospels preserve separate memories of a hurried, joyful morning. They can be fitted together in more than one way, and none of them requires an error.
fit.short: Mary Magdalene probably ran to Peter before the angel spoke, met Jesus alone at the tomb, and the other women met Him on their way.

scene.label: “Rejoice!”
scene.text: Jesus used the ordinary Greek greeting, the word people said when they met on the street. It literally means “rejoice,” and on this morning the everyday greeting said exactly what had happened.

scene.label: Holding His feet
scene.text: To fall down and take hold of someone’s feet was a gesture of deep respect and urgent appeal, as when the Shunammite woman “caught him by the feet” before Elisha (2 Kings 4:27). The women held a real body, not a vision.

scene.label: Worship received
scene.text: When Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet, Peter lifted him up (Acts 10:25–26), and an angel refused John’s worship (Revelation 22:8–9). Jesus does not refuse the women. He receives worship as only God may.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew alone records this meeting on the road. The angel’s message becomes a meeting with Jesus Himself, and the call to Galilee is repeated, preparing for the mountain where Matthew’s Gospel ends (28:16–20). Matthew often notes that people worshiped Jesus, from the wise men (2:11) to the disciples in the boat (14:33); now the women worship the risen Lord.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is risen in a body that can be held, and He accepts worship that belongs to God alone. His first instruction reaches the men who deserted Him, and He calls them His brethren.
seeing.living: Jesus did not wait for the women’s fear to fade before He sent them; He met them while they were still running “with fear and great joy” and gave them a message to carry. That message was for men who had failed Him. If you have run from Jesus, hear what He sent them: you are still His brother or sister, and He still means to meet you.
seeing.ponder: Where have you failed Jesus, and can you believe that He still calls you His own and wants to meet you?

preaching.big_idea: The risen Jesus meets His messengers and claims the deserters as His brothers.
preaching.watch_for: Matthew sets two reports side by side. The women run to tell the disciples the truth (28:8–10), and “while they were going” the guards go to the chief priests and are paid to spread a lie (28:11–15).
